strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing multi-agent LLM benchmarks (GT-Bench, MAgIC, LLMArena) are text-only, while existing VLM agent benchmarks are single-agent. VS-BENCH is, to the authors' knowledge and as far as the related-work section establishes, the first benchmark combining visual observations with multi-agent strategic interaction.

The environment suite is well-curated and principled: eight games span cooperative (Hanabi, Overcooked), competitive (Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong), and mixed-motive (Coin Dilemma, Monster Hunt, newly proposed Battle of the Colors) interactions, each grounded in recognized game-theoretic or MARL settings with a clear formal reward-structure definition of each category.

The two-axis evaluation design (offline next-action prediction for strategic reasoning; online normalized episode return for decision-making) is sensible and lets the authors disentangle theory-of-mind ability from long-term optimization ability, yielding distinct and interesting findings (e.g., reasoning models win on reasoning but some open-source models rival them in mixed-motive games due to prosocial behavior).

Evaluation is broad: fourteen VLMs across commercial reasoning, commercial chat, and open-source tiers, with careful per-model configuration details (Table 3) including exact API versions and explicit disclosure of why o3 and gemini-2.5-pro were excluded.

The analyses add value beyond a leaderboard: the multimodal vs. text-only comparison (Finding 3, that images can hurt performance) is a notable insight about current VLMs; CoT/test-time-scaling analysis, social-behavior radar plots, and concrete failure cases (information asymmetry in Hanabi, rule misunderstanding in Overcooked) provide actionable diagnostics.

Reproducibility appears strong: dataset construction is documented per environment (400 samples each, with explicit balancing principles and strategy mixes in Appendix C), decision-making protocols, reward structures, and raw unnormalized results (Table 4) are all provided, and code/data are promised for release.
weaknesses: The offline 'strategic reasoning' ground truth is strategy-dependent and partially circular: datasets are generated from specific agent policies (minimax with particular depths for Breakthrough, three fixed alpha values for Kuhn Poker, hand-crafted heuristics for mixed-motive games, and notably trajectories of two specific VLMs — o4-mini and doubao-1-5-thinking-pro — for Atari Pong). Prediction accuracy therefore measures how well a model predicts those particular agents' styles, not general strategic reasoning; a model could score low for being differently strategic. The 'oracle=100' framing overstates what these labels represent.

Statistical support for decision-making results is thin: only 10 self-play episodes or 10/20 games per setting, with extremely large standard deviations reported in Table 2 (e.g., o4-mini Hanabi 42.9±30.5, claude-3-7-sonnet Poker 92.9±22.7, Breakthrough ±47). Rankings of models separated by a few points are likely unstable, yet the paper draws tier-level conclusions from these noisy averages.

The claim that VLMs 'fail to extract visual information' (Finding 3) rests on multimodal underperforming text-only in three environments. Since the text descriptions are complete state encodings, multimodal inputs add perceptual noise but no missing information, so this comparison conflates perception difficulty with information content; the conclusion, while plausible, is stronger than the evidence.

Limited evaluation breadth in places: only three open-source models, and the decision-making protocol pits VLMs against a single conventional opponent per competitive game (one MCTS configuration, one CFR setting, the built-in bot), limiting generality of conclusions about adversarial play.

Presentation issues that should be fixed: repeated typo 'Comptitive' in table headers, an empty URL in the abstract ('available at .') and Appendix C, and Figure 11/12 caption inconsistencies (Frame 4 labeled 'Frame 1'). The Hanabi visual observation includes deduced hint annotations under each card, which arguably simplifies the theory-of-mind challenge relative to the true game.

No human baseline is included (acknowledged in limitations), so it is hard to calibrate whether 47.8% prediction accuracy or 24.3% return constitutes a meaningful gap or near-human performance in these specific environments.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing VLM agent benchmarks are predominantly single-agent or text-only, and VS-BENCH is a well-motivated attempt to evaluate VLMs on strategic reasoning and decision-making in multimodal multi-agent settings. The formalization as Partially Observable Markov Games with multimodal observation and text action spaces is clean.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: eight vision-grounded environments spanning cooperative (Hanabi, Overcooked), competitive (Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong), and mixed-motive (Coin Dilemma, Monster Hunt, Battle of the Colors) games cover a meaningful spectrum of multi-agent interaction structures, and each game is well-grounded in the game theory/MARL literature.

The evaluation is broad and multi-dimensional: offline next-action prediction accuracy and online normalized episode return are complementary, and the evaluation of fourteen leading VLMs (reasoning, chat, and open-source) provides a useful snapshot of the field's capabilities.

The dataset construction principles (predictable, diverse, balanced) are explicitly stated and per-environment dataset generation procedures are documented in detail (Appendix C), supporting reproducibility. Limitations are candidly acknowledged in Appendix A (two-player focus, no human baseline, single metrics).

The analysis sections yield genuinely interesting observations, particularly the finding that text-only observations outperform multimodal input in several games (Fig. 3, Tables 5-6), suggesting VLMs fail to extract useful information from visual game states, and the social-behavior analysis showing prosocial strategies of open-source models in social dilemmas.
weaknesses: There is a circularity concern in the strategic reasoning datasets for some environments: the Hanabi data is 90% generated from mutual prediction between two reasoning VLMs, and the Atari Pong ground-truth actions are the next actions of o4-mini and doubao-1-5-thinking-pro themselves. This means models are partly predicting other VLMs' idiosyncratic behaviors rather than grounded strategic play, which may bias the benchmark in ways that are not well analyzed.

The online decision-making evaluation is statistically underpowered: only 10 self-play episodes (or 10/20 games against conventional agents) per environment per model, with reported standard deviations as large as ±30 to ±47 (e.g., o4-mini Board 30.0±47.0, Poker 69.3±32.9). Many model rankings, including several of the paper's headline findings, may not be statistically distinguishable at this sample size, and no significance testing is reported.

Some headline findings are largely predictable or previously established: reasoning models outperform chat models, CoT prompting improves performance (Finding 4), and models are far from optimal. These confirm expectations rather than offering surprising insight, which limits the analytical contribution beyond the benchmark itself.

The noise-to-signal ratio in the decision-making results is concerning: many models score at or below random in most environments, and the environment-level aggregation of very heterogeneous returns (zero-sum outcomes vs. process rewards) into a single 'normalized episode return' may obscure rather than clarify model capabilities.

Important strong models are absent from the evaluation (o3, gemini-2.5-pro due to cost/rate limits), which weakens the claim of evaluating 'fourteen state-of-the-art' models at the frontier; several evaluated models (grok-2-vision, Llama-3.2-90B) are already dated relative to the May 2025 cutoff.

The benchmark's visual grounding is relatively shallow for several environments: for Kuhn Poker, Hanabi, and the grid-world games, the visual observations are essentially rendered symbolic state (text and chips in an image), so the claimed distinction from text-only multi-agent benchmarks is weaker than suggested; the finding that text-only input beats multimodal input partially undermines the paper's core motivation.

Presentation and rigor issues: the code/data URL is empty in the abstract; 'Battle of the Colors' is a game designed by the authors rather than a recognized environment, and its properties (e.g., optimal policy choice) deserve more justification; the Hanabi observation includes annotations of 'all possible colors and ranks deduced from received hints,' a design choice that materially changes the game's difficulty and is not ablated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing VLM agent benchmarks are predominantly single-agent, while existing multi-agent LLM benchmarks are text-only. The framing around cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions is well grounded in game theory and MARL literature.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: eight vision-grounded environments adapted from well-recognized settings (Hanabi, Overcooked, Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong, plus three social dilemmas), evaluated along two complementary dimensions (offline next-action prediction and online normalized episode return), with random and oracle normalization for interpretability.

The evaluation breadth is substantial: fourteen commercial and open-source VLMs spanning reasoning, chat, and open-source categories, with precise version pinning (Table 3) and honest disclosure of models excluded due to cost/rate limits.

The analysis section goes beyond leaderboard reporting: multimodal vs. text-only comparisons (Finding 3, that multimodal input can hurt performance, is a notable and counterintuitive result), test-time scaling with CoT, behavioral visualization of social dilemma play, and qualitative failure cases (Appendix F) are informative.

The appendix is thorough: dataset construction principles, per-environment reward engineering (e.g., firework return for Hanabi, step reward for Pong to handle sparsity), and detailed environment specifications support reproducibility and scrutiny.
weaknesses: Circularity in the strategic reasoning ground truth undermines the headline metric. For several environments the 'ground truth' next actions are generated by VLMs themselves: Hanabi samples come from mutual prediction between two reasoning VLMs, and the entire Atari Pong dataset uses actions from o4-mini and doubao-1-5-thinking-pro as labels. Measuring VLMs' ability to predict other VLMs' behavior is not the same as measuring strategic reasoning, and the 'oracle = 100' framing is misleading when the oracle is itself an evaluated model. This weakens Finding 1.

The online decision-making evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Only 10 self-play episodes (or 20 games vs. MCTS, 10 runs of 120 poker hands) are used, and the resulting variances are enormous (e.g., o4-mini Hanabi 42.9±30.5, gemini-2.5-flash Hanabi 27.1±36.0, Poker values with ±50-60). Many per-cell differences in Table 2 are not statistically meaningful, and model rankings in Fig. 1 (right) could flip under resampling. Claims such as 'reasoning models achieve relatively better results' need stronger support.

Self-play with two instances of the same model in cooperative and mixed-motive games conflates coordination ability with shared inductive biases. Identical agents may coordinate through correlated defaults rather than genuine theory-of-mind, which the paper's interpretation (e.g., Finding 5 on prosocial behavior) does not fully disentangle.

The 'optimal' agents used for normalization are heuristic rather than provably optimal in several environments (e.g., 'always move to the middle block and wait' in Monster Hunt; a depth-5 minimax in Breakthrough, which the authors themselves note is not guaranteed optimal). The 0-100 normalization therefore does not correspond to true optimal return, complicating cross-environment comparability.

Reproducibility gaps in the current manuscript: the code and data URL in the abstract and Section C is literally blank ('available at .'), which is a material omission for a benchmark paper whose core contribution is release and adoption.

Some evidence breadth is thin relative to the claims: the multimodal vs. text-only and CoT analyses cover only three environments, and prompting sensitivity (single prompt per environment) is unexamined, despite known prompt variance in LLM game-playing.

Minor but concerning inconsistencies: the text claims failures concentrate in 'Overcooked, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong, and Monster Hunt, three of which are adapted from video games' (that is four games and Kuhn Poker is a card game); 'Comptitive' typo in Table headers; the number of episodes/protocol details are scattered across the appendix. These do not invalidate the work but suggest insufficient polish for the evidentiary burden a benchmark must carry.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing VLM agent benchmarks are single-agent, while existing multi-agent LLM benchmarks (GT-Bench, MAgIC, LLMArena) are text-only. VS-BENCH is the first systematic multimodal, multi-agent benchmark spanning cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive dynamics.

The three-dimensional evaluation design (perception, strategic reasoning, decision-making) is well motivated and diagnostically useful; the finding that models have strong perception (best 84.9%) but large gaps in reasoning (46.6% next-action accuracy) and decision-making (31.4% normalized return) cleanly isolates where the weakness lies.

The evaluation is extensive and credible: 15 state-of-the-art VLMs across three categories, ten environments curated from established MARL/game-theory literature, plus analyses that go beyond leaderboard reporting (text-only vs. multimodal ablations, CoT/test-time scaling, persona effects on social behavior, failure mode taxonomy).

The human study (26 participants) provides a valuable calibrated baseline, showing humans (62.7) roughly double the best model (o3, 31.4) — this grounds the benchmark's difficulty claims in a meaningful reference point rather than only oracle numbers.

The appendices are unusually thorough and reproducibility-oriented: exact model versions and API settings, per-game perception/reasoning dataset construction procedures, reward definitions, raw unnormalized returns with standard deviations, and released code/data. The ethics statement also thoughtfully addresses dual-use risks and human-subject protections.

Table 1's taxonomy of required abilities (spatial perception, theory of mind, long-term planning, team collaboration) per environment gives future users a principled way to interpret per-game results rather than treating the aggregate score as monolithic.
weaknesses: The strategic reasoning ground truth is substantially derived from VLM agents' own actions (e.g., trajectories of o4-mini, doubao-1.5-thinking-pro, doubao-1.5-vision-pro) or hand-designed heuristic policies. Accuracy therefore partly measures agreement with a particular class of (often noisy or suboptimal) policies rather than prediction of optimal or human play, which weakens interpretation of 'theory-of-mind' claims and could bias evaluation toward or against certain models. This circularity concern is not thoroughly discussed.

The decision-making evaluation sample sizes are small: only 10 self-play episodes per model (and 10 games as each side for Breakthrough), and the text in Section 4.4 confusingly states gpt-4.1's overall return as both 4.8 (Table 4) and 4.4. With 10 episodes and the very large variances visible in Table 6 (e.g., o4-mini ±30 on normalized Hanabi), many model rankings — and the red/green highlightings in Tables 3 and 4 — may not be statistically reliable. No significance tests or confidence intervals on the headline comparisons are reported.

Several environment adaptations introduce arbitrary, non-standard reward shaping that complicates comparability with prior literature: the weighted Pong step reward (0.9/0.9 mix of survival time vs. score), the 'firework return' variant for Hanabi, and heuristic 'optimal' baselines in MPE and the grid-world games. These choices mean 'normalized return' is benchmark-specific and the oracle normalization is only as strong as the chosen reference agent (e.g., a minimax agent for Breakthrough is explicitly not guaranteed optimal).

The main result that multimodal input yields worse performance than text-only observations (Fig. 3, Tables 7–8) is intriguing but only analyzed on three of ten environments with six reasoning models; the paper's own conclusion that this shows VLMs 'fail to extract visual information' is asserted rather than experimentally disentangled from confounds such as context length, prompt design, or coordinate-overlay wrappers.

Only three open-source VLMs are evaluated, and several frontier models (claude-4-opus, grok-4, deepseek-r1) are excluded for cost or modality reasons; while justified in Appendix B, this limits the generality of claims about 'open-source vs. commercial' gaps.

Presentation issues slightly undermine polish: 'DeepMined' cited as the Gemini author, 'contributions are threefold' typed as 'threshold' in the introduction, 'Comptitive' in table headers, blank repository URLs in the reproducibility statement, and the Figure 6 text reporting gpt-4.1's return inconsistently (4.4 vs. 4.8 in Table 4).

Novelty is primarily in curation and benchmark assembly rather than methodological insight; the individual environments and metrics largely reuse existing settings, so the paper's contribution rests on the quality of assembly and analysis — which is solid but not conceptually deep.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing VLM agent benchmarks are overwhelmingly single-agent and/or text-only, while strategic multi-agent interaction with visual observations is largely unevaluated. The framing via cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive dynamics is well motivated.

The evaluation is broad and systematic: ten environments spanning three interaction types, fifteen models (commercial reasoning, commercial chat, and open-source), and three complementary evaluation dimensions (perception, next-action prediction, normalized episode return). This triangulation is more informative than a single metric.

The analysis sections add substantial value beyond a leaderboard: multimodal vs. text-only comparisons, CoT/test-time scaling effects, persona manipulations in social dilemmas, a human baseline (26 participants, 62.7 vs. o3's 31.4), and qualitative failure modes (e.g., ignoring information asymmetry in Hanabi, over-adjustment in Pong). These make the benchmark diagnostically useful.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: exact model versions are listed, per-game dataset construction, reward functions, normalization schemes, and observation formats are documented in detail (Appendices C–I), and code/data release is promised.

The finding that some open-source models match reasoning models on mixed-motive games due to prosocial behavior, and that personas significantly shift behavior, is an interesting empirical observation.
weaknesses: The strategic reasoning 'ground truth' is partly circular: labels for several games (KAZ, Atari Pong, MPE) are the next actions of other VLM agents, and Hanabi labels are generated from mutual prediction between two reasoning models. The benchmark thus measures the ability to predict VLM-style (not human or optimal) behavior, which weakens the claim of evaluating 'theory-of-mind' ability and may favor models with similar play styles to the label-generating models.

The 'oracle' agents used for normalization are frequently heuristic rather than optimal: the MPE optimal baseline is simply a heuristic value of 0, and the Coin Dilemma 'optimal' agent only collects its own color (arguably suboptimal for self-interest play). Normalized returns (random=0, oracle=100) are therefore not guaranteed to have consistent meaning across environments, complicating cross-game aggregation into a single 'overall' score.

Decision-making evaluation is noisy and thin: only 10 self-play episodes (20 games vs. MCTS in Breakthrough) per model per environment, with very large standard deviations visible in Table 6 (e.g., gemini-2.5-flash 31.2±11.4 on Hanabi; qwen-vl-max 5.8±39.6). No statistical significance tests are reported for the many ranking claims.

Several environments are heavily simplified in ways that undercut the 'vision-grounded, real-world-like' motivation: KAZ is capped at five zombies with coordinate axes overlaid, Pong receives coordinate overlays and step-survival rewards weighted 0.9/0.1 that reward mere survival over play quality, and Overcooked is a 4x5 grid with 50-step episodes. The gap between these sanitized visuals and the paper's real-world claims deserves more candid discussion.

Open-source coverage is limited to three models, and notable contemporary models (claude-4-opus, grok-4, deepseek) are excluded; the cost-based exclusion rationale is understandable but limits the generality of conclusions about the open-source vs. commercial gap.

Some text/figure inconsistencies reduce confidence: Table 10 appears identical to Table 4 for o3 (fine, but the human-normalized presentation should clarify this); the claim that Overcooked, Atari Pong, and Monster Hunt 'are all adapted from video games' is imprecise since Monster Hunt is a 5x5 grid world; typos such as 'Comptitive' in table headers.

The text-only ablation conclusion ('VLMs can fail to extract visual information') is drawn from only three environments; a broader ablation would be needed to support this as a general finding about multimodal processing failures.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap in the literature: existing VLM agent benchmarks are predominantly single-agent or text-only, while existing multi-agent LLM benchmarks (GT-Bench, GAMA-Bench, MAgIC, LLMArena) are text-only. VS-BENCH is a well-motivated first step toward vision-grounded multi-agent evaluation.

The evaluation scope is substantial and comprehensive: ten environments spanning cooperative (Hanabi, Overcooked, KAZ), competitive (Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong, MPE), and mixed-motive (Coin Dilemma, Monster Hunt, Battle of the Colors) dynamics, with a clear taxonomy (Table 1) mapping games to required abilities.

The three-dimensional evaluation protocol (perception / strategic reasoning / decision-making) is a thoughtful design that decouples coupled failure sources, and the finding that models perceive well (67.8-84.9%) yet reason and decide poorly (best: 46.6% prediction, 31.4% return) is a clear, actionable contribution.

The analysis section goes beyond leaderboard reporting: multimodal vs. text-only ablations (Fig. 3, Tables 7-8), CoT/test-time scaling effects (Fig. 4), social behaviors and persona sensitivity (Fig. 5, Table 9), human experiments with 26 participants (Table 10), and qualitative failure mode analysis (Appendix G) give the community real diagnostic insight.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed dataset construction procedures (400 samples per environment with balancing and sampling strategies in Appendices C-D), reward specifications for all environments (Appendix E), raw unnormalized results (Table 6), and released code/data.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with extensive appendices that document model versions, prompts, and environment rules in reproducible detail.
weaknesses: Decision-making results are based on very few episodes (e.g., 10 self-play games, 20 Breakthrough games) and the reported standard deviations are large (e.g., o3 55.8±20.9 in Hanabi, 80.0±40.0 in Breakthrough in Table 8). No statistical significance tests are provided, so many model rankings in Tables 4 and 8 may not be meaningful, and conclusions like 'some open-source models achieve comparable results to reasoning models' rest on noisy point estimates.

The strategic reasoning proxy (next-action prediction accuracy) is only loosely tied to theory-of-mind ability, and the 'oracle = 100' framing is questionable: ground-truth labels are frequently generated by other VLMs' actions (KAZ labels from o4-mini/doubao trajectories, Pong from o4-mini, Hanabi 90% from mutual prediction between two reasoning models). Predicting such labels reflects behavioral mimicry as much as strategic reasoning, and mimicking suboptimal agents may not indicate stronger ToM.

Decision-making is evaluated via self-play for most games, meaning both players use the same model. Self-play may mask competitive weaknesses (both agents err symmetrically), does not test adaptation to diverse opponent populations, and partially conflates environment-solving ability with strategic interaction. The authors acknowledge this limitation but it substantially affects the interpretation of the headline decision-making numbers.

Some normalization choices are ad hoc: the MPE 'optimal' baseline is a heuristic value of 0, Pong mixes score and survival rewards with a 0.9/0.1 weighting, and models scoring below the random baseline in competitive games (e.g., grok-2-vision at -58.2 in MPE, Table 6) raise questions about whether normalization punishes negative returns consistently across environments.

The environments are largely curated from existing MARL/game-theory benchmarks with visual wrappers added; the environmental novelty is modest (Battle of the Colors is the main new environment), so the contribution is primarily the evaluation framework and empirical study rather than new environments or methods.

Minor presentation issues that should be fixed: 'our contributions are threshold' (p.2), repeated misspelling 'Comptitive' in Table headers, inconsistency between Fig. 6 (gpt-4.1 = 4.4) and Table 4 (4.8), a citation typo ('Google DeepMined'), and Table 1's ability-star ratings lack explicit definitions in the main text.

The text-only vs. multimodal comparison is limited to three environments; since the paper's central premise is that visual observations matter in multi-agent settings, a broader ablation would better support the claim that multimodality is the bottleneck rather than strategic reasoning per se.
